title: Hydrogen from petroleum reservoirs, with the other products left underground

concept.text: The proposed innovation would turn a petroleum reservoir into a hydrogen-producing reactor and containment system. Oxygen would be injected to support underground heating and reactions involving hydrocarbons, and hydrogen would be recovered selectively while reaction coproducts remained underground. A September 2019 CBC report describes this goal in work involving the University of Calgary and Proton Technologies, including laboratory work and small field tests. That report does not establish the complete capability at sustained operating scale.

The defining capability combines underground conversion, transport of hydrogen to a recovery point, selective separation, and retention of the remaining products. Generating a hydrogen-bearing gas is only one part of that result. The reservoir would have to deliver a useful hydrogen stream without allowing unacceptable coproduct production, leakage, or loss of hydrogen within the formation.

significance.text: If sustained selective recovery and coproduct retention were demonstrated, hydrocarbons left in the rock could become a source of hydrogen without first being extracted and delivered to a surface conversion plant. The reservoir would supply both the reaction environment and the place where other products were retained. The 2019 report describes the intended use of oil remaining underground and compares the approach with surface steam-methane reforming.

Conditional implications: successful operation could create another use for some residual hydrocarbon resources, including potentially suitable heavy-oil or depleted reservoirs. It would not establish that abandoned wells or reservoirs generally make suitable reactors. Reservoir chemistry, connectivity, existing well condition, containment, and the energy needed to operate the process would determine where the capability was practical.

Impact limits: selective hydrogen recovery alone would establish neither low cost nor low lifecycle emissions. Those outcomes would also depend on oxygen production, heating and compression requirements, hydrogen losses, coproduct containment, and long-term operation. Hydrogen pipelines, markets, and end uses are downstream possibilities outside the petroleum-engineering breakthrough. The analogy to a surface hydrogen plant is therefore useful for understanding the product, but it does not establish equivalent process control, efficiency, or commercial performance.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is reliable operation of an underground reaction-and-separation system across a heterogeneous reservoir. Hydrogen must move from its generation zone to the recovery system at a useful rate. The 2019 CBC report explicitly identifies transport through the reservoir as something still requiring verification at that time; laboratory generation and small field tests did not settle that question.

Engineering synthesis, rather than a verified account of the cited reviews: the proposed thermal route would require control of the heated reaction zone, distribution of injected oxygen and any steam, and pathways through which hydrogen and coproducts move. Preferential flow could bypass intended reaction volumes or carry injected fluids elsewhere. Hydrogen consumption or trapping within the formation could reduce recovery. Separation would have to operate with the actual reservoir fluid mixture and operating conditions. These are concrete questions for demonstrating the concept; the supplied retained scientific texts do not establish their severity or show that they have been solved.

The supplied research attributes optimized hydrogen-production temperatures above 700 °C for methane and 500–700 °C for light oil, heavy oil or bitumen, and oil shale to a 2025 Next Energy review. It also names in-situ combustion, gasification, and the water-gas shift as relevant reaction pathways. These details remain unverified in the supplied review: the retained Next Energy copy contains only a redirect, without article text or confirmed document identity. The temperature ranges should therefore be treated as reported values awaiting verification, not universal requirements or demonstrated reservoir operating windows.

A further integration barrier is demonstrating selective recovery together with containment. The earlier research mentions a palladium membrane operating on a prepared laboratory gas mixture, but the supplied evidence does not verify that result. Even a verified prepared-mixture test would establish performance only under its tested conditions; it would leave open reservoir transport, durability with actual fluids, and retention of the remaining products.

current_state.text: The supported historical account is the September 29, 2019 CBC report. It describes University of Calgary and Proton Technologies work on oxygen injection, underground hydrogen generation, and selective recovery, reporting laboratory work and small field tests. A larger, semi-commercial pilot was planned for the following year. That was a prospective plan, and hydrogen transport through the reservoir still required verification. The article is evidence of early development, not evidence that the planned pilot subsequently achieved sustained production and containment.

The supplied research describes two 2025 reviews as identifying unresolved feasibility and commercialization challenges. It attributes scale-up difficulties and limited understanding to Optimizing hydrogen generation from petroleum reservoirs, and a need to establish viability and competitiveness to In situ hydrogen generation in subsurface reservoirs of fossil fuels by thermal methods. Those descriptions cannot be independently confirmed from the supplied retained evidence: the first article was not captured, and the Applied Energy copy contains only a redirect. The original research reports abstract-level information, but the supplied review could not verify the abstracts. This limits the use of those assessments without showing that they are false.

The earlier research also mentions company claims about membrane purity and future production tonnage, and a separate 2025 microbial trial said to have produced hydrogen-rich gas without a reported production rate. No supporting company statements or microbial-trial report were supplied for verification. Consequently, these mentions establish neither measured thermal-process performance nor a sustained field demonstration. Gas composition alone would not establish hydrogen throughput, and a microbial route would require its own assessment rather than serving automatically as evidence for oxygen-driven thermal conversion.

The supplied evidence does not establish whether a later sustained, metered field campaign with an adequate material balance had been published, or whether commercialization had occurred, by November 1, 2026. The freshness search record is empty. The defensible conclusion is that the documented 2019 work was preliminary and that subsequent status remains unresolved here; absence of retained evidence is not evidence that no later demonstration exists.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration, not an established standard: operate one defined reservoir pattern for months, producing a continuously measured hydrogen stream at a useful rate and purity selected before the trial. Report cumulative hydrogen recovery, interruptions, injected fluids, operating conditions, and the surface energy and material inputs needed to sustain production. Duration and acceptance thresholds should be justified for the intended application rather than presented as universal benchmarks.
completion_criteria.label: Months of hydrogen production meeting preselected rate and purity

completion_criteria.text: The same demonstration should quantify retention of a preselected fraction of reaction coproducts through a material balance with stated uncertainty. It should account for injected and produced fluids, relevant initial and final inventories, and carbon in applicable gas, liquid, dissolved, and solid phases. Gas analyses and reservoir pressure would contribute to that assessment but would not alone establish closure. A carbon balance would address carbon-bearing products; retention claims for other substances would require corresponding measurements.
completion_criteria.label: Material balance quantifies preselected coproduct retention with stated uncertainty

completion_criteria.text: A convincing result should distinguish hydrogen generation from hydrogen recovery, characterize transport and separation under actual reservoir conditions, and document evidence for containment during operation and an explicitly defined follow-up period. A membrane test on bottled synthesis gas, or a combustion pilot reporting only hydrogen percentage, would not establish this combined result. Flow rate, cumulative recovery, coproduct accounting, and uncertainty are essential to interpreting performance.
completion_criteria.label: Hydrogen generation distinguished from recovery, with reservoir containment demonstrated

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: independently assess the measurements and repeat operation in additional reservoir settings selected to test meaningful differences in geology, fluids, and well configuration. Report where performance deteriorates and what operating limits apply. Such trials could establish demonstrated breadth and practical suitability within tested conditions; finite tests would not establish universal reservoir applicability or indefinite containment.
completion_criteria.label: Independent measurement assessment and repeated reservoir trials document operating limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison with PET-11, In-reservoir conversion of bitumen to pipeline-specification crude: both concepts involve conversion within a reservoir. Their intended recovered products distinguish them: PET-06 targets hydrogen with coproduct retention, whereas PET-11's supplied title targets pipeline-specification liquid crude. Only PET-11's title was supplied, so its detailed chemistry, separation requirements, and development status cannot be compared.

Roster-based comparison with PET-04, Industrial in-situ conversion of oil-shale kerogen, and PET-09, Bitumen that flows at native reservoir temperature: these share an interest in changing how difficult hydrocarbons can be used or recovered. PET-04 concerns underground conversion of kerogen, while PET-09 concerns bitumen mobility at native temperature. PET-06 adds the distinct requirement of generating and selectively recovering hydrogen while retaining coproducts. Their titles do not establish shared operating methods or equivalent maturity.

Roster-based comparison with PET-01, Blind prediction of multiphase reservoir flow, and PET-08, Permeability and saturation measured through the reservoir volume: prediction and measurement of subsurface flow could help evaluate reactant distribution, hydrogen transport, and containment in PET-06. They concern understanding reservoir behavior; successful prediction or measurement would not by itself demonstrate underground hydrogen production.

Roster-based comparison with PET-02, Conventional-oil recovery at gas-field recovery factors, PET-05, Shale-oil recovery from the matrix, and PET-03, Commercial gas production from methane hydrate: these concern recovering hydrocarbon resources in different forms and geological settings. PET-06 instead proposes converting hydrocarbons underground and recovering hydrogen. Improved oil recovery or commercial hydrate production would not establish selective hydrogen recovery or coproduct retention.

Roster-based comparison with PET-07, Deep well construction without a steep depth penalty, and PET-10, A pressure plan with a prospectively tested earthquake bound: well construction and pressure management could affect access, operation, and containment for an underground reactor. They remain separate capabilities. PET-06 does not imply either reduced deep-well costs or a demonstrated earthquake bound.

Technical synthesis: PET-06 also overlaps with membrane engineering and geological storage. Membrane engineering addresses selective separation; geological storage addresses retention and monitoring. The proposed petroleum-engineering advance requires these capabilities to function together with reservoir conversion and transport, so success in either adjacent field alone would not complete PET-06.

unresolved_issues: The 2025 Next Energy temperature ranges, reaction-pathway discussion, and bibliographic identity require verification against usable article text.

The recommendation to remove all unverified technical specifics was not adopted in full: useful temperature values and engineering questions were preserved with explicit attribution or synthesis labels, as requested. Their qualification does not resolve the underlying evidence gaps.

The contents and bibliographic details of the two other cited 2025 reviews remain unverified from the retained materials. The research names Chengdong Yuan, Pavel Afanasev, Aysylu Askarova, Evgeny Popov, and Alexey Cheremisin as the Applied Energy authors, but the supplied review could not confirm that list.
No supplied primary evidence resolves the prepared-mixture palladium membrane result, company purity and tonnage statements, or the separate 2025 microbial trial.
Whether a subsequent field campaign or commercialization result existed by November 1, 2026 remains unresolved; no freshness evidence was supplied.
Acceptable hydrogen rate, purity, recovery fraction, coproduct-retention fraction, uncertainty, follow-up duration, and practical operating boundaries remain application-specific proposed choices.
The detailed relationships to other roster entries remain provisional because only their IDs and titles were supplied.

brief.title: Hydrogen from oil left underground
possible: People could get hydrogen fuel from oil left in underground rock, while keeping the other reaction products below the surface. Injected oxygen would help heat the oil and release hydrogen, which special filters would separate for recovery.
why: Oil that remains underground could supply hydrogen without first being pumped out and taken to a surface processing plant. The surrounding rock would provide both the reaction space and storage for the other products.
This could give some depleted oil fields and heavy-oil deposits another use as hydrogen sources.

sources.cited_for: It addresses the difficulty of turning underground hydrogen generation into a larger working system.
sources.not_established: A review does not demonstrate sustained hydrogen recovery and retention of other reaction products in a reservoir.

sources.cited_for: Early tests support underground hydrogen generation using oxygen injection.
sources.not_established: The tests did not establish sustained useful hydrogen recovery together with containment of the other reaction products.

sources.cited_for: It addresses whether underground hydrogen production could become a practical, competitive process.
sources.not_established: A review does not establish a working reservoir system or its commercial performance.

sources.showed: This review discusses natural underground hydrogen and methods for converting oil and gas into hydrogen underground, including reaction pathways and temperatures.
sources.cited_for: It addresses the reactions and heating involved in underground hydrogen generation.
sources.not_established: Reported reaction temperatures do not establish workable conditions across an actual reservoir.

shown: University of Calgary and Proton Technologies researchers reported laboratory work and small field tests in 2019. These supported hydrogen generation underground, but left a central question open: whether enough hydrogen could travel through the rock to be recovered.
missing: Sustained production must deliver hydrogen at a useful, continuously measured rate and purity.
Measurements must account for how much hydrogen reaches the wells and how much stays trapped or is consumed underground.
Separation must work with actual underground fluids while the other reaction products remain contained.
Repeated trials must establish which reservoir conditions support reliable operation.

milestones.label: Months of hydrogen production at agreed rate and purity
milestones.explanation: A reservoir trial would have to deliver measured hydrogen for months at a useful rate and purity chosen beforehand, with operating inputs tracked. This would establish sustained production.

milestones.label: Measured retention of other reaction products
milestones.explanation: The same trial would have to account for materials entering, leaving and remaining underground, with stated uncertainty and a retention target chosen beforehand. This would test whether other products stay underground.

milestones.label: Hydrogen recovery and underground containment demonstrated together
milestones.explanation: A trial would have to distinguish hydrogen made from hydrogen recovered, test transport and separation, and track containment through a defined follow-up period. This would demonstrate the combined system.

milestones.label: Independent assessment and repeated trials establish operating limits
milestones.explanation: Independent assessment of measurements and trials in additional reservoir settings would have to identify where performance holds or deteriorates. This would establish the system’s practical range.

uncertain: Useful production rates, purity, retention targets and follow-up periods depend on the intended application.
How strongly uneven flow, hydrogen loss and changing underground conditions would limit recovery remains open.
Low cost and low overall emissions would depend on energy inputs, hydrogen losses and long-term containment.

page.title: In situ hydrogen generation with coproduct retention
page.definition: Thermal reactions generate hydrogen inside an oil or gas reservoir. A separator installed downhole, inside a well, recovers hydrogen while the other reaction products remain underground.

goal.need: In 2023, global hydrogen production emitted 920 million tonnes of CO₂. Retaining reaction carbon underground targets production-site emissions, which the IEA estimates at 75–95% of total emissions from conventional fossil-based hydrogen. Upstream emissions still require separate accounting.

figures.caption: IEA lifecycle emission intensities for hydrogen production without carbon capture.
figures.note: CO₂-equivalent includes the warming effects of greenhouse gases other than CO₂.

statements.quote: extract hydrogen from existing oil reservoirs, while carbon dioxide will remain trapped in the ground.
statements.context: The announcement released on 24 June 2020 describes the intended Proton Technologies process approved for the Saskatchewan Petroleum Innovation Incentive.

statements.quote: This technology adapts commercial hydrogen selectivity membrane technology for downhole deployment in wellbores for in-situ hydrogen production by gasification.
statements.context: The Hygenerator project description concerns front-end engineering and design for a demonstration pilot. The page was last modified on 23 December 2024.

completion.title: A field system recovers hydrogen downhole while retaining the other reaction products underground.
completion.criterion: An integrated system operates in an actual hydrocarbon reservoir: thermal conversion generates hydrogen, hydrogen reaches a production well, and a downhole separator delivers it to the surface while the other reaction products remain underground. Measurements of produced fluids and reservoir inventories establish selective recovery and coproduct retention within stated uncertainties. The cited goals specify no minimum hydrogen rate, product purity, run duration or numerical retention fraction.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; a qualitative field test following the published selective-recovery goal.
completion.basis: Searches of Saskatchewan SPII and NRCan project documents, the Canadian hydrogen standards roadmap, ISO catalogue descriptions and Proton/ProtonH2 publications found no reservoir-specific integrated acceptance test specifying rate, purity, duration and retention. The criterion follows the original selective-recovery goal. ProtonH2’s current process description claims 15–20% CO₂ retention and permits surface separation; that developer claim is not peer reviewed.

milestones.title: Laboratory experiments demonstrate hydrogen generation from reservoir feedstocks at TRL 3.
milestones.criterion: Technology readiness level (TRL) 3 requires experimental proof of a critical function. Oil: Tang et al., published on 17 September 2026, tested one Liaohe heavy-oil sample; three runs per condition gave a mean 10.84 mol% H₂ at 450 °C for 6 h under nitrogen, with 1:1 oil/water by mass; gas composition excludes water and nitrogen. Natural gas: Rui et al., published on 2 November 2022, reported up to 26.63 mol% H₂ from methane, air and water at 600 °C and 50 bar after 10 h; replicate counts were not reported.
milestones.set_by: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, general TRL 3 definition, also used in NRCan’s hydrogen roadmap. It supplies a maturity criterion without a reservoir-specific hydrogen-yield cutoff.

milestones.title: A membrane assembly selectively recovers hydrogen in laboratory validation at TRL 4.
milestones.criterion: TRL 4 requires laboratory validation of technological components. Shared separator evidence is a University of Calgary report dated 19 May 2017: one experiment with 10% H₂/90% CO₂ at 280 °C and 1 MPa reported a hydrogen flux of 0.979 cm³ cm⁻² min⁻¹ during an approximately 15-minute test. Gas-volume reference conditions and analysed product purity are unspecified. This prepared-mixture experiment establishes neither oil-reservoir nor natural-gas-reservoir fluid performance. The report is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, general TRL 4 definition, applied to the separator assembly. It specifies laboratory validation without prescribing hydrogen purity or flux.

milestones.title: An integrated hydrogen-production prototype works in a simulated reservoir environment at TRL 6.
milestones.criterion: TRL 6 requires demonstration of a system or subsystem model or prototype in a simulated environment. A near-final production prototype couples hydrogen generation, transport and selective separation under representative reservoir conditions. Oil and natural gas: no published result establishing this integrated stage was located.
milestones.set_by: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, general TRL 6 definition. Its application here concerns the integrated production and separation system; the framework supplies no reservoir-specific operating conditions.
milestones.threshold_quote: prototype demonstration in a simulated environment

milestones.title: A hydrogen-generation and downhole-separation prototype works in a reservoir field test at TRL 7.
milestones.criterion: TRL 7 includes prototype field testing. A prototype demonstrates hydrogen generation, transport to a production well and selective downhole recovery in an actual reservoir. Oil: Proton’s presentation dated 24 March 2021 claims a membrane test with field-produced gas containing H₂S, but gives neither a test count nor evidence of downhole installation; the claim is not peer reviewed. Natural gas: no corresponding prototype field-test result was located.
milestones.set_by: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, general TRL 7 definition. The field-test stage concerns production and separation; reservoir-wide coproduct retention is assessed in the completion test.

not_found: No reservoir-specific numerical milestone acceptance criteria were located; the published TRL definitions provide general development stages.
No field result establishing selective downhole recovery together with full coproduct retention was located for either reservoir feedstock.
